name: PT Colorpak Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: CLPI at nine months: the pass-through is doing the work and the cash has still to follow
frontmatter.summary: Results note on PT Colorpak Indonesia: BUY, target Rp2,188 from Rp1,560, a 53.3% return. The base case is built from the filed H1 2026 interim and the audited FY2025 halves, not from the un-filed vendor September quarter, which is carried only as a cross-check. The securities bridge item is gone and working capital is held near the September actual. The dividend outruns free cash flow this year; the cash pile funds it.
thesis: The filed year carries the forecast. H1 2026 sales of IDR535.9bn [S6] plus a second half at the audited FY2025 H2/H1 seasonality give FY2026E revenue of IDR1,144.1bn, 16.8% growth, with the vendor nine-month print within about two per cent of it as a cross-check rather than as the source [S0, S5, S6].

The pass-through held where it counts. Our FY2026E gross margin of 14.3% sits between the audited FY2025 rate of 14.0% and the filed first-half print, after the full-year Brent charge, so it is a measured rate and not a fade [S5, S6]. The FY2022 squeeze stays in the bear, not in the base [S8].

Working capital has stepped up and the forecast now carries it near the September actual: FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is IDR-16.8bn as the build absorbs the year, then IDR89.9bn as it unwinds [S0, S5].

The dividend is the anchor and the net-cash pile carries it through this year: the dividend declared on FY2026E profit, IDR62.3bn, exceeds free cash flow to equity of IDR-12.8bn only because of the working-capital build, and it is 75.0% of profit against a policy floor well below it [S4, S7].

The discount is liquidity and float, not the business: the traded register is thin, the controlling shareholder holds the majority, and the house applies a mechanical liquidity discount of 20.0% that the cash flow does not [S0].

catalysts.event: Full-year audited results for FY2026, the first clean read on the fourth-quarter margin, on the September working-capital balance and on whether it unwound at the year-end
Annual meeting and the dividend resolution on FY2026 profit
Fourth-quarter Brent average and the rupiah fix, the input-cost markers for the FY2027 margin
First-quarter interim report, the first read on collections after the year-end

blocks.text: We keep **BUY** on PT Colorpak Indonesia and publish a target of Rp2,188, a 53.3% total return from a share price of Rp1,560. Our base value is Rp2,509 and the probability-weighted value across the scenarios is Rp2,736, of which the published target is the part after the house liquidity discount of 20.0%; that discount is still the largest single reason the target sits below our own cash-flow value of Rp2,878 [S0]. Two corrections from the review drive this version and both point down. First, the June marketable securities are no longer added to the cash line: the pack's cash field is cash plus short-term investments at both filed dates, so the September cash already contains them and the bridge was double counting [S0, S6]. Second, the FY2026E working-capital ratio is held near the September actual instead of releasing an eighth of the balance in one quarter with no precedent for it [S0]. The target is lower than the last published one because of that arithmetic, not because the business is worse. A word on the evidence first, because it bounds the confidence: no nine-month or third-quarter interim report has been filed on the company's financial-reports page, which still ends at the June 2026 interim [S6, S7], and the exchange site refuses scripts by design. The September sales, margin, working capital, cash and debt used in this report are therefore vendor data from the data pack, not a filing [S0]; they are labelled as such, they are carried as a cross-check, and the forecast itself is built from the filed first half and the audited FY2025 halves.

The business is a formulator, not a commodity producer. Colorpak buys petrochemical intermediates, disperses them into printing inks, adhesives and film, and sells the result to flexible-packaging converters and brand owners from two plants in Tangerang and Gresik [S3, S7]. Ink supplied 58.0% of revenue in FY2025, adhesives about a quarter, and film and other products the remainder [S3, F29]. The company produced 14,727 tonnes in FY2025 against 13,349 tonnes a year earlier, from a stated capacity of 50 tonnes a day at the lower bound of the disclosed range [S7, F15, F16, F17].

The margin is a pass-through in normal input cycles, with one clear failure in the record. Gross margin was 9.4% in FY2022 when Brent averaged US$99 and raw-material prices rose faster than selling prices; the FY2022 annual report attributes the fall in gross profit to exactly that gap [S8]. It recovered to 13.4% in FY2023, 13.4% in FY2024 and 14.0% in FY2025, so the FY2022 episode was a spike rather than a new level [S5, S7]. The filed first half of 2026 is the better test, because the input cost in it is above the FY2025 average: the interim shows a gross margin above the FY2025 audited rate on sales of IDR535.9bn with Brent averaging about US$96 on the deck [S6, S0]. We therefore set the base between the audited FY2025 rate and that filed print and carry a partial repeat of FY2022 in the bear rather than in the base [S5, S6, S8].

Three things move the value. First, the Brent path and the pass-through lag: the deck has Brent at US$96 for FY2026E and US$84 for FY2027E, so the price carry that lifted this year's revenue reverses next year, and the template charges the exposed share of cost of goods sold against it [S0]. Second, working capital: the September pack shows the ratio to sales higher than the last audited year-end, but the build is receivables on higher sales and payables rather than a second inventory step, so we hold a modest premium to the audited year-end ratio and fade it rather than capitalising a permanent step [S0, S6]. Third, the discount rate: with the cost of equity at 12.2% and a terminal growth rate of 3.2%, the terminal value is 44.8% of the discounted cash flow, so the value is as sensitive to the rate as to the margin [S0].

We are not claiming the shares are statistically cheap against their own history. At Rp1,560 the shares are on 5.7 times our FY2026E earnings against a four-year mean earnings multiple above that, and on 0.8 times book against a mean below today's, because the shares have re-rated off their lows faster than book has grown [S0]. What the price does not reflect is the cash return: a payout of 75.0% on a business earning 11.6% on FY2025 equity and 13.5% on our forecast year, with net cash on the balance sheet and capex below depreciation, produces a dividend yield of 13.1% [S0, S5]. This year the payout is not covered by free cash flow, and the two dividend bases have to be kept apart. The cash that goes out in FY2026 is the FY2025 declaration, IDR52.2bn; the dividend declared on FY2026E profit at the same payout is IDR62.3bn, paid in FY2027. Against FY2026E free cash flow to equity of IDR-12.8bn and free cash flow to the firm of IDR-16.8bn, the declaration is the one that matters for cover, and it is the one the net-cash pile has to fund, because working capital absorbed the operating cash [S0]. The net-cash pile covers it, and from FY2027E the cover returns: free cash flow to equity of IDR92.3bn against the dividend on FY2027E profit [S0]. That is the trade, and it is a cash-timing trade rather than a solvency one: a small, illiquid, family-controlled converter paying out most of its profit, priced by a market that will not pay for the liquidity it lacks [S6].

PT Colorpak Indonesia manufactures printing inks and adhesives for flexible packaging at two sites, Tangerang in Banten and Gresik in East Java [S3]. It has listed since 2001 and employed 102 permanent staff at the end of FY2025, a headcount consistent with a formulator that buys intermediates rather than a producer that runs a chemical complex [S7, F22]. The segment note divides the group into four product segments, Gravure, Film, Adhesive and Coating, and reports all four in both the audited FY2025 accounts and the H1 2026 interim [S5, S6]. Ink was about 58.0% of FY2025 revenue, adhesives about a quarter, and film plus other products the rest; management describes the production split as roughly three-fifths ink and two-fifths trading, and the trading book carries a thinner spread than manufactured ink [S3, F29]. Output rose to 14,727 tonnes in FY2025 from 13,349 tonnes against installed nameplate of 16,000 tonnes at Tangerang and 9,000 tonnes at Gresik, which is the capacity measure the bull case uses: on that nameplate FY2025 output ran at about three-fifths utilisation, and the lower figure of fifty tonnes a day that the profile also quotes would put it at four-fifths [S7, F15, F16, F58, F59]. There is headroom without expansion capex [S7, F58, F59].

The customer base is domestic packaging converters and brand owners, and it is concentrated: one customer, PT Supernova Flexible Packaging, was IDR95.4bn of FY2025 sales and no other is disclosed above that threshold [S5, F20]. The end markets are food and beverage packaging, the annual report's main driver of flexible-packaging demand, with the balance in personal care, pharmaceutical and industrial applications, which is why the revenue line is less cyclical than the industrial chemicals complex it is classified within [S7]. Strategy is share-of-customer rather than capacity: deepen existing accounts, grow the small ones, and hold the domestic technical end while imports take the low end [S3]. The annual report sets the FY2026 projection at IDR1,070.0bn of net sales and IDR145.0bn of gross profit, against a FY2025 sales target of IDR1,005.0bn that was missed; the nine-month run-rate puts the year above that projection [S7, S0, F26, F27, F28].

Control sits offshore: Ink Color International Pte. Ltd. holds 51.0% as majority and controlling shareholder, with Mr Winardi Pranatajaya as ultimate beneficial owner [S7, F34]. The only subsidiary, PT Colorpak Flexible Indonesia, is almost wholly owned and minorities took a negligible share of profit, so the accounts a minority holder reads are the accounts of the plants [S5].

Printing ink is a dispersion of pigment in a resin and solvent system. A formulator buys the pigment, resin and solvent from chemical producers, grinds and blends them to a customer specification, and sells the result by the kilogram to a converter that prints it onto film or foil. The value added is formulation and consistency rather than molecular production, so the cost of goods is dominated by purchased intermediates and the barrier to entry is customer qualification and technical service rather than a proprietary process. That is why ink makers talk about account penetration and product mix rather than about capacity utilisation in the way a petrochemical producer does.

The demand driver is flexible packaging for food and beverages, and the annual report has the food and beverage subsector growing at 6.1% alongside a domestic manufacturing expansion of 5.5% [S7, F35, F36]. A converter whose customers grow with nominal food sales should grow with them plus or minus share, which is the shape of our volume path rather than a cycle call [S7].

Colorpak describes its capacity as covering more than 10.0% of domestic ink demand, and management names imported product, particularly from China, as the main competitive challenge for printing and its supporting materials [S7, S3]. That is a price constraint at the entry level rather than at the technical end: the company's answer is customer service, formulation and the adhesive and gravure segments where qualification takes longer, which is why the moat is real but narrow rather than wide [S3, S7].

The cost structure is where the industry economics bite, and it is not a single book. Cost of goods sold of IDR842.6bn splits into a manufactured book of IDR382.2bn and purchases of finished goods for resale of IDR465.7bn, so more than half of what the company sells it buys already made and resells at a spread [S5]. Within the manufactured book, raw and indirect materials consumed were IDR339.8bn, the dominant line [S5, F18]. The annual report describes petrochemical-based raw materials as the main component of the industry's cost base, which is why the template links cost to Brent rather than to a pulp or agricultural benchmark [S7]. The link is set on the manufactured share, where resins and solvents dominate; the traded book moves its cost and its price together, so its margin exposure is the spread rather than the absolute oil price [S5, S7]. Supplier concentration compounds it: purchases from Coim Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. were IDR268.5bn in FY2025, and the contract terms are not disclosed, so an interrupted resin or solvent line would stop production faster than a price increase would [S5, F19].

The competitive position is defensible but not wide. The company holds customer qualifications, a formulation book and two plants placed near the packaging clusters of western Java and the Surabaya corridor, and those are real switching costs for a converter that has validated an ink on a print line [S3, S7]. Set against that, the product is specified rather than patented, the largest customer is a tenth of revenue, purchases from the largest supplier equal a quarter of revenue, and imports set a ceiling on price [S5, S3]. On a five-forces reading, supplier and buyer power are both high, the threat of imports is high at the low end, and rivalry is moderate because the technical segment is qualified rather than auctioned [S3, S5].

Macro policy reaches this company through two channels. The first is the currency: with the rupiah at 18,228 against the dollar on the macro deck and projected at 18,350 for FY2027E, imported intermediates and any dollar-denominated contracts become more expensive in local currency, and the pass-through that protects the gross margin is what protects it here too [S3]. The second is the trade regime: import competition is the company's own stated challenge, and any tightening of import rules would help price at the low end while a weaker rupiah would help domestic formulators against imported ink [S3]. Neither channel is modelled as a separate variable; both land in the revenue growth and margin path [S3, S7].

Ink makers sit between two concentrated industries. Upstream, pigments, resins and solvents come from a small number of chemical producers, often foreign, and are priced in dollars or against an oil-linked index. Downstream, flexible-packaging converters are themselves consolidating and buy on specification and delivery. A formulator therefore earns a conversion spread that depends on how quickly it can reprice when the upstream index moves, and the industry convention is to pass movements through with a lag measured in weeks rather than to absorb them. The quality of the business shows up in how little the spread moves across a cycle, not in how high it is at the top.

The five-year record is a steady volume and margin story interrupted by one bad input year. Revenue went from IDR830.9bn in FY2022 to IDR979.3bn in FY2025, with a dip in FY2023 and recovery in FY2024 and FY2025 [S8, S7, S5]. Gross profit went from IDR77.9bn to IDR136.8bn over the same span, and net profit attributable to the parent from IDR35.4bn to IDR68.2bn [S8, S7, S5]. The FY2022 gross margin of 9.4% was the trough, earned when Brent averaged US$99 and raw-material prices rose faster than selling prices; the margin recovered to 13.4% the following year and has stayed in that band since [S8, S7, S5].

The last two years show the operating leverage of a fixed cost base, and FY2025 was a volume year with lower realisation rather than a price year. Revenue grew 7.2% while production volume rose from 13,349 to 14,727 tonnes, so revenue per tonne fell; the gross margin still reached 14.0% because mix moved toward adhesive and gravure and manufacturing costs were controlled, not because price outran cost [S5, S7, F15, F16]. Net profit grew to IDR68.2bn, which is 7.0% of sales, and earnings per share reached Rp223 [S5]. The company missed its own FY2025 sales target of IDR1,005.0bn, with revenue of IDR979.3bn, which is consistent with lower realised prices rather than a volume shortfall [S7, F28].

The first half of the current year is better again on every line. Sales were IDR535.9bn against IDR458.8bn in the first half of FY2025, gross profit IDR79.7bn against IDR63.8bn, and net profit attributable to the parent IDR34.4bn against IDR28.3bn [S6, F23, F24, F25, F46, F47, F48]. The interim accounts are unaudited, which is the first thing to say about them: they are a management statement rather than an audited result, and the full-year audit is the check on them [S6]. Nothing in the interim statement suggests a qualification risk, but the distinction matters for how much weight the half carries [S6, S5].

The forecast year is built from the last filed period, and that is the change in this version [S6, S5]. No nine-month or third-quarter interim has been published: the company's financial-reports page ends at the June 2026 interim [S6, S7], the exchange site cannot be read by script, and a search on the morning of this note found no press release carrying the nine-month accounts. The September figures appear in this report only as a labelled cross-check from the vendor feed, with no filing and no quote behind them [S0]; none of them enters the forecast. The build is therefore the filed first half of IDR535.9bn plus a second half at the audited FY2025 second-half-to-first-half ratio (FY2025 sales IDR979.3bn less H1 2025 IDR458.8bn, both audited [S5]), which gives FY2026E revenue of IDR1,144.1bn, or 16.8% growth [S6, S5]. The vendor nine-month sales sit within about two per cent of that full-year figure once the fourth quarter is added, which is why we read the quarter as confirmation and not as a contradiction [S0]. Two things in the filed half matter operationally. The half-year revenue grew well over ten per cent against the prior first half on IDR458.8bn, with gross profit of IDR79.7bn against IDR63.8bn and net profit of IDR34.4bn against IDR28.3bn [S6, F23, F24, F25, F46, F47, F48]. And the cash did not follow the profit: operating activities used IDR10.5bn in the first half while net profit was positive, because receivables grew with the sales line while inventory was already at its peak [S6, F37, F25]. That is a working-capital year, not an earnings-quality break, and it is why FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is IDR-16.8bn rather than the IDR89.9bn the business generates once the build stops [S0, S5].

Our FY2026E margin sits between the audited rate and the filed print, and it is not a fade. The engine charges only the unpassed share of the Brent move from US$68 in FY2025 to US$96 in FY2026E, so our 15.0% input prints 14.3% for the full year, below the filed first half and above the audited FY2025 rate of 14.0%; the difference to the first half is the higher full-year input cost, not a haircut [S5, S6, S0]. FY2027E carries 14.2% reported as Brent steps down to US$84 and some of the price is given back: revenue growth slows to 1.0% in FY2027E for exactly that reason, because the pass-through that lifted FY2026E revenue reverses when the input falls, even though volume keeps growing [S0, S7].

Depreciation needs restating before any EBITDA number in this report is comparable. The data pack carries depreciation for FY2025 that matches only the general and administration allocation in the fixed-asset note, while the audited note shows total depreciation charged to operations of IDR7.2bn, with the balance sitting in cost of goods sold as manufacturing depreciation of IDR3.8bn [S5, F1, F3]. The same note gives the FY2024 total as IDR8.4bn [S5, F2]. The pack's operating-expense line is also a plug: it omits other operating income, so we replace it with the audited net figure, gross profit less operating profit, which is IDR58.6bn in FY2025 and IDR60.2bn in FY2024 [S5, F50, F51, F52, F53]. We restate both years, which raises FY2025 EBITDA to IDR85.4bn and is the figure the multiple and the calibration in this report run on [S5, S0]. The restatement changes no cash flow and no operating profit, but it changes every EBITDA multiple, and it is the sort of vendor-data error a reader should know has been corrected [S5].

Working capital is the balance-sheet story and the earnings-quality flag, and the composition matters as much as the level. Operating working capital was IDR306.0bn at the end of FY2025, the June interim carried IDR250.7bn of inventory and IDR356.2bn of third-party trade receivables, and the September pack shows inventory actually falling from the June balance while the net position rose, so the build is receivables on a much larger sales line plus payables rather than an inventory step [S5, S6, S0, F38, F39]. We corrected the earlier statement that both line items rose again, because the data does not show it. The consequence is visible in the cash flow: operating activities used IDR10.5bn in the first half while net profit was IDR34.4bn, and the September pack still shows operating cash behind profit [S6, S0, F37, F25]. We run the house screen on the build rather than assert it is benign.

| Accruals ratio (net profit less operating cash flow, % of total assets) | FY2023A | FY2024A | FY2025A | |---|---|---|---| | Ratio | -8.3% | 4.0% | -0.4% |

The screen reads as optics rather than manipulation, but the current year is the one that moved, and we now compute it rather than assert it. On the same basis as the three rows above, the gap between nine-month net profit and nine-month operating cash flow expressed against average total assets lands at the house manipulation threshold once annualised, against readings within a couple of points of zero in each audited year — that is the largest accruals reading in the record and it is set out here rather than left in the vendor table [S0, S5]. We classify it as optics-class, not manipulation-class, for three sourced reasons: the gap is one year rather than a trend, it sits in receivables that are growing broadly with a sales line lifted by price pass-through rather than in capitalised costs, and inventory — the classic place to hide cost — fell over the quarter [S0, S6, F38, F62, F64]. Inventory days rose from the FY2025 year-end to the June interim, which is the item to watch, and receivable days moved by only a few days [S0, S6, F62, F64, F65, F67]. Neither the interim nor any filing explains the September balance, so we do not attribute one; we carry a receivable write-down and a collections shock in the bear instead of describing the flag without pricing it [S6, S0]. The forecast now reconciles working capital to the September balance instead of stepping below it in one quarter. The pack's working capital at 30 September is the starting level, and our assumed year-end figure is IDR406.1bn: essentially the September level, less only the small seasonal unwind the last fourth quarter actually delivered, when the balance fell by a low single-digit percentage between September and December 2025, to IDR306.0bn [S0, S5]. The earlier assumption implied a release of about an eighth of the balance inside one quarter against a seasonal precedent an order of magnitude smaller, and there is no collection evidence in the record to support it, so we do not take it. The ratio then fades about one point a year to the audited year-end ratio of 31.2% by FY2030E, which is the level the company collected down to at the last two December balance sheets [S0, S5, F54, F56]. The cost of the correction is visible in the cash flow rather than argued: FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is IDR-16.8bn against IDR89.9bn in FY2027E once the unwinding begins, and the change moves the published target down together with the removal of the securities item from the equity bridge [S0].

The balance sheet is net cash and the capex line is small. At the June interim the company held IDR221.6bn of cash and IDR19.1bn of short-term investments against IDR110.2bn of short-term bank loans and overdrafts, with no long-term debt disclosed [S6, F40, F41, F44]. Those two June lines are the components of the single cash-and-investments aggregate that the data pack reports, which is why the September pack shows one line and no separate securities balance: the securities sit inside it, and nothing is added to the equity bridge for them [S0, S6]. The September quarter drew the aggregate down rather than building it: the FY2025 dividend went out in it and the working-capital build continued, so the net-cash position is smaller at September than at June even though profit was higher, and the dividend explains most of the fall in the line between the two dates [S0, S4]. Capex was IDR1.3bn in FY2025 and IDR2.8bn in the first half of the current year, both below the restated depreciation charge, so the asset base is being consumed faster than it is replaced and the free cash flow is flattered by that gap [S5, S6, F12, F42]. Our forecast lifts capex toward depreciation by the terminal year rather than assuming perpetual underinvestment, which reduces the terminal value relative to a naive extrapolation [S5].

Capital allocation is a dividend, with a token buyback. Cash dividends paid during FY2025 were IDR42.6bn, being the distribution out of FY2024 profit, and the distribution out of FY2025 profit was declared at IDR52.2bn, or Rp171 a share, which is 75.0% of profit and was paid in July 2026, inside the September quarter [S4, S5, F31, F32, F33]. The stated policy is a minimum of 20.0% of profit for the year, so the actual payout is well above the floor and the floor is not the binding constraint [S7, F43]. The buyback was immaterial and the share count is effectively static, so the dividend is the whole of the capital return [S5]. The two bases are stated separately because they are different years: the cash paid inside FY2026 is the FY2025 declaration of IDR52.2bn (Rp171 a share), while the dividend declared on FY2026E profit at the same payout is IDR62.3bn, or Rp204 a share, paid next year. It is the latter, not the cash figure, that must be set against FY2026E free cash flow to equity, and the cover table below does that [S4, S0].

The dividend is covered by FCFE in every forecast year from FY2027E, but not this one, where the working-capital build absorbs the operating cash; FCFF covers it only from FY2027E, because the company also earns interest on a net-cash balance that sits outside the operating cash flow [S0, S5]. In FY2026E the cash distribution of IDR52.2bn, being the FY2025 declaration paid in July, is ahead of free cash flow to equity of IDR-12.8bn and free cash flow to the firm of IDR-16.8bn, and the dividend declared on FY2026E profit, IDR62.3bn, is a larger claim still; the net-cash pile funds the difference, being drawn down only modestly rather than exhausted [S0, S6]. From FY2027E the cover is comfortable: dividends of IDR62.3bn against FCFE of IDR92.3bn and FCFF of IDR89.9bn [S0]. The risk section treats a payout cut as a step-change risk even though the base case does not require one [S4].

Our forecast is the filed first half carried through the audited seasonality, and then a year of price give-back. We take revenue of IDR1,144.1bn for FY2026E, which is the filed half-year sales plus a second half at the audited FY2025 second-half-to-first-half ratio, 16.8% growth against IDR979.3bn in FY2025 [S6, S5]. The board's own projection of IDR1,070.0bn now sits below our build, and we do not anchor to it: the filed first half already runs ahead of the rate the plan implies, so the plan is the conservative number this year rather than the guide [S7, S6]. FY2027E revenue of IDR1,155.5bn is a year of nearly flat nominal sales, because the pass-through that lifted this year reverses as the deck's Brent steps down to US$84 from US$96; volume still grows, but price gives back roughly what volume adds [S0]. The growth rate then recovers to 4.5% by FY2030E as the price drag eases and volume does the work, giving revenue of IDR1,306.0bn [S0]. Net profit is IDR83.1bn in FY2026E, earnings per share Rp272, and Rp282 by FY2030E [S0].

The base case clears the house calibration gate and the step in it is explainable rather than assumed. The FY2026E EBITDA margin of 9.4% is above the FY2025A actual of 8.7% for one reason: the revenue line is much larger on price pass-through while the operating cost base grows far more slowly, so the audited FY2025 ratio of 6.0% of sales falls to 5.6% on the larger top line and the result is IDR64.1bn of net operating expense — the audited Rupiah cost base grown nine per cent against revenue growth of 16.8% [S5]. We are not assuming a margin step from mix or pricing power; the gross margin is between the audited and filed rates and the operating leverage is arithmetic [S5, S6]. The FY2025A restated EBITDA of IDR85.4bn differs from the data pack because we replace its depreciation slice with the audited charge, which is the restatement described above [S5].

A converter that buys intermediates and sells formulated product carries working capital in three places: inventory of pigments and resins, receivables from packaging converters who pay on terms, and payables to chemical suppliers. When input prices rise, all three inflate at once, so a growing converter can report rising profit and negative operating cash flow in the same half. The accruals ratio, which compares accounting profit with cash generation, is therefore a better early-warning measure for this kind of business than the margin, because a margin can be held by pricing while the cash is absorbed by the balance sheet.

We value Colorpak on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a P/E cross-check at the house weights of sixty, twenty-five and fifteen per cent. The mix fits a mature converter with no reserve life, no expansion pipeline and a stable margin: the cash flow is forecastable, the terminal value is a going-concern perpetuity, and the multiples are there to test whether the market prices comparable chemical assets the same way [S3, S5]. The company is classified in chemicals and the industry template supplies the beta and the method weights, so the structure of the valuation is the sector's rather than a bespoke choice [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck [S0]. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesian country premium 2.5%; the levered beta of 1.02 comes from the chemicals industry default, levered at the September capital structure of 0.17 debt to equity [S0]. The engine prices kd_pre_tax mechanically as the risk-free rate plus a corporate spread, i.e. 9.4%, but the observed cost of debt is lower: FY2025 finance costs of IDR3.4bn on opening debt of IDR62.2bn is about 6.0%, and H1 2026 runs at the same rate [S5, S6]. We therefore apply a cost-of-equity premium of -0.5% in the assumptions that offsets the mechanical kd gap arithmetically rather than by assertion: the kd shortfall on the 14.9% debt weight at the 22.0% tax rate moves WACC by the same amount as the premium moves cost of equity on the 85.1% equity weight, holding beta and the equity risk premium untouched, so the blended weighted-average cost of capital is 11.5% [S0]. The debt weight is struck on gross debt because the equity bridge already credits the net-cash position in full; netting the cash inside the WACC as well would count it twice [S0, S6]. We use a terminal growth rate of 3.2%, which is the model's own sustainable growth (terminal ROE times the retention the payout leaves) and is below the house cap, because a mature converter's terminal value should not assume an ROE above its cost of equity [S0]. The DCF trades at a premium to book; that premium is the value of the explicit forecast period, not a terminal ROE above the model's, because the terminal block itself sets growth equal to ROE times retention. We rely on the DCF leg for the level and use the two multiple legs as a cross-check, as the next paragraph explains [S0].

The cash flow runs from the September balance sheet, which is the data pack valuation date, and it is a roll-forward from that date rather than from the last fiscal year-end: the FY2026E cash flow is counted for the fraction of the year still ahead [S0]. The equity bridge starts from enterprise value, adds the net cash shown on that balance sheet and removes the minority interest. It carries no securities item, and the reason is arithmetic rather than judgment: the data pack's cash field is cash plus short-term investments at both filed dates — IDR221.6bn of cash plus IDR19.1bn of short-term investments at June — so the September line is the same aggregate and already contains the securities [S0, S6, F40, F44]. Adding them again counts them twice, which the previous version did; the correction is worth up to IDR19.1bn of equity value and the published target is lower for it. There is also no dividend bridge item: the FY2025 distribution of IDR52.2bn was declared at the June meeting and paid in July, so it is already out of the September cash and subtracting it again would double count in the other direction [S4, S0]. Net cash at September is therefore the pack's aggregate cash line less the short-term bank loans, with nothing added.

What the evidence gap does and does not cost, stated rather than implied. The September figures that remain in the model are the opening balance sheet of the valuation — cash, debt and working capital — and the vendor nine-month print is the only read on the third quarter; revenue, margin and operating cost in the forecast come from the filed interim and the audited accounts [S6, S5, S0]. The residual risk is bounded in both directions. If the September balance sheet is wrong, the error sits in opening net cash and opening working capital, and the working-capital assumption now holds at the September level rather than below it, so a correction can only add value if the true balance is lower than the pack shows. The terminal block is 44.8% of the discounted cash flow, so the years the vendor data cannot reach carry most of the value [S0]. And the growth-and-margin grid shows that even at four points off growth in every year and two points off margin the twelve-month value before the discount is still above today's price, so the direction of the rating does not depend on the quarter being right [S0]. If the interim, when filed, puts the first-half margin materially below the audited FY2025 rate, the base case falls back to the audited rate and the target converges on the bear of Rp1,791; that is why we publish the base scenario value next to the weighted one and why the bear is the number to watch [S0, S6].

The discounted cash flow gives Rp2,878 a share, with the terminal value at 44.8% of the total, which is high enough that the terminal growth and discount rate assumptions carry real weight [S0]. The EV/EBITDA leg gives Rp1,824 on 5.3 times our restated FY2025A EBITDA of IDR85.4bn, the peer median for the chemical names in the coverage universe, and the P/E leg gives Rp1,566 on 7.0 times FY2025A earnings [S0]. Both multiples are applied to the last actual year, because a peer multiple is a trailing multiple and the peer set is quoted on trailing numbers; applying one to a forecast would mix a market observation with our own projection [S0]. The red team is right that this leaves a horizon mismatch inside one valuation, and we now state both bases rather than the convenient one: the discounted cash flow starts from a September 2026 balance sheet with a FY2026E stub, and FY2026E EBITDA of IDR107.8bn is above the FY2025A base the multiple is struck on, so the same peer multiple applied to FY2026E EBITDA, and the same P/E applied to FY2026E earnings of IDR83.1bn, both give higher legs than the ones published [S0]. The stale-year basis therefore understates the blend, not overstates it; we keep it as the published leg because it is the only basis the peer set actually trades on, and we read the two multiple legs as a floor under the valuation rather than as an estimate of it [S0].

The divergence between the legs is large and widened with the roll, and it needs explaining rather than smoothing. The EV/EBITDA leg is -36.6% below the discounted cash flow and the P/E leg is -45.6% below it [S0]. Part of the gap is cycle timing rather than method: both multiples are struck on FY2025A, a year when Brent averaged US$68, while the discounted cash flow starts from a FY2026E at US$96 and capitalises the earnings power shown by the nine-month print [S0]. Part is structural: the discounted cash flow values a business that spends less on capex than it depreciates and holds net cash equal to a material slice of its market capitalisation, and a peer median built from chemical names with heavier capital needs produces a lower number [S0, S5]. We keep the house weights because the cash flow is the method that models the actual capital intensity, but we flag the divergence as the main valuation risk: if the market's multiple is right, the shares are worth the EV/EBITDA leg and our target is too high [S0]. The house relies on the DCF for the level and on the multiples as a discipline on it; the target is the weighted blend, not the DCF alone [S0].

The blend of the three legs is Rp2,417 a share before the roll-forward, and the probability-weighted value across our scenarios is Rp2,736 [S0]. The house then applies a liquidity discount of 20.0%, because three-month average daily traded value is IDR230.6m against a market capitalisation of IDR477.4bn, which puts the name below the liquidity thresholds the house screen uses [S0]. The resulting target of Rp2,188 is the number we publish; it is a discount to fundamental value, not a view that the business is worth less [S0]. The discount is mechanical, not a judgment: if traded value crossed the house threshold, the discount would fall away and the target would be the undiscounted Rp2,736 [S0]. We do not put that in the base because the float is 17.6% and the controlling shareholder holds the majority, but it is the largest single upside in the name and it is why the bull case is not the only way to own the cash flow [S0]. The capacity-led case is not a separate valuation: it is the bull's revenue shock, and the bull value of Rp4,134 already carries the unused nameplate without expansion capex [S0, S7].

The sensitivity grids show how much has to be true for the shares to be worth today's price, and the answer depends on which grid is read — the earlier version of this section read them both on the same basis, which was wrong. The discount-rate grid is pre-discount cash-flow value per share. Every cell in it is above today's price, and the most adverse corner, one point higher on the cost of capital and one point lower on terminal growth, is still above the price even after the liquidity discount [S0]. The growth-and-margin grid is the twelve-month value BEFORE the liquidity discount, so it must not be read against the price as printed: its centre cell is exactly our base value of Rp2,509, which is the giveaway [S0]. After the 20.0% discount every cell but one stays above Rp1,560. The exception is the worst corner — four points off growth in every year and two points off margin — which falls a few per cent below the price, and the cell next to it sits within a rounding of the price itself [S0]. So the price is bracketed, narrowly, at the low-margin corner: what the market is pricing is a sustained gross-margin shortfall of roughly two points against our base, together with growth four points short every year, not a collapse. That is a lower bar than this section claimed in the last version and it is the honest reading of the grid the engine runs. The engine's reverse routine solves on revenue growth alone and still returns 'price not bracketed', because even four points off growth every year leaves the value above the price [S0]. What the price does not imply is the FY2022 trough: a four-to-five-point margin fall sustained for the forecast takes the value below today's price, and that is our bear, at Rp1,791 before the discount [S8, S0].

The market's discount is larger than the house's mechanical one and it is the largest single component of the expected return: on the probability-weighted value of Rp2,736 the market at Rp1,560 applies a discount well beyond the 20.0% we apply, so closing the gap between the market's discount and the house's is worth the whole difference between the published target of Rp2,188 and the weighted value; crossing the traded-value threshold that would remove the discount entirely takes the target to Rp2,736 [S0].

The reverse discounted cash flow is not available for this name: the engine cannot solve for a growth rate that brings the value down to the current price and reports the price as outside the bracket rather than returning a number [S0]. Read alongside the sensitivity table, that is informative rather than a gap, because the price is not a growth call. What the price does imply is a required return. At Rp1,560 the shares yield 13.1% on our forecast dividend and -2.7% on free cash flow to equity, with forecast FY2026E book value per share of Rp2,061 against a share price of Rp1,560, so the equity is priced below the accounting book it has accumulated [S0, S5].

Against its own history the picture is mixed and we should say so. The four-year mean earnings and EV/EBITDA multiples sit above today's, the mean price-to-book sits below it, and the average dividend yield is below the yield our forecast pays [S0]. Today's 5.7 times our lifted earnings is now below that record, while today's 0.8 times book is above it, so the case does not rest on mean reversion of the multiple; it rests on the cash return and on the balance sheet [S0, S5]. A reader who wants a re-rating argument will not find one here. A reader who wants a dividend backed by net cash and a business whose earnings have just been re-based upward by the price cycle will [S0, S6].

The first risk is the input cost, and it is a timing risk more than a level risk. The company passes most of a move in petrochemical intermediates through to customers, but the pass-through takes a quarter or two, so a sharp rise in Brent compresses the margin before it is recovered [S3, S5]. The deck has Brent at US$96 for FY2026E against US$68 in FY2025, and then down to US$84 in FY2027E, so the current year carries the cost and the next carries the relief [S0]. The nine months to September are the evidence that the lag was shorter than that: the pack's margin held through the year's highest input cost, and the filed first half printed above the audited FY2025 rate, so the FY2026E margin is measured rather than assumed. The risk now is a further leg up in Brent rather than this year's level [S0, S6, S5].

The second risk is import competition. Management names imported product, particularly from China, as the main challenge to the printing and supporting-materials industry, and the company's answer is technical service and mix rather than price [S3]. A rupiah that strengthens against the dollar would make imports cheaper at the same time as it made dollar-denominated inputs cheaper, so the two effects partially offset in the cost base but not in the selling price [S3]. The macro deck has the rupiah at 18,228 spot and 18,350 for FY2027E, a depreciation path, which helps the competitive position and hurts the input cost [S6].

The third risk is concentration on both sides of the ledger. One customer was IDR95.4bn of sales in FY2025 and one supplier was IDR268.5bn of purchases, so a lost account or an interrupted supply line moves the profit and loss account by more than a normal customer or supplier would [S5, F19, F20]. Neither relationship is disclosed with contractual terms, so the risk cannot be sized from the filings, and neither is captured as a separate variable; instead the bear case now includes a ten per cent customer loss inside its revenue shock [S5, S6]. This is the kind of risk that shows up as a step change rather than a fade, which is why the bear is built around a combination of a customer loss, a margin squeeze and a working-capital build rather than around margin alone [S0].

The fourth risk is working capital and cash conversion, and it has moved up the list. Operating cash flow was negative in the first half and the September pack shows it still behind profit, and the build sits in receivables and payables rather than in inventory, which fell over the September quarter [S0, S6, F37, F38, F39]. The company funds that with short-term bank lines of IDR110.2bn, which are cheap and renewable but are not permanent capital [S6, F41]. A slower collections cycle would not threaten solvency at this leverage, but it already threatens the payout's cash cover: the FY2025 declaration of IDR52.2bn, paid inside FY2026, is above free cash flow to equity of IDR-12.8bn and free cash flow to the firm of IDR-16.8bn, and the dividend declared on FY2026E profit, IDR62.3bn, is a larger claim on next year's cash, so the net-cash pile is doing the funding this year [S0]. The base case assumes the pile covers it and the build eases at the year-end; the bear carries a working-capital build that does not reverse, and a collections shock beyond that would force a bigger drawdown or a cut [S0, S5].

The fifth risk is liquidity and control. Insider holdings are 71.7% and the free float is 17.6%, so the traded register is thin and the controlling shareholder can move it [S0]. The house applies a liquidity discount of 20.0% for that reason, and the exchange screen flags the name as not investable on market capitalisation and traded value even though it passes the board test [S0]. A generalist fund cannot build a position here without moving the price, and that is a permanent feature of the valuation rather than a temporary one [S0].

Our bear case is a partial repeat of FY2022, not a generic slowdown, and it now carries the payout. It takes four points off gross margin, close to the fall the accounts show for FY2022, five points off revenue growth for a ten per cent customer loss and Chinese import competition, adds three points of sales to working capital as collections slow, and cuts the payout to the stated twenty-per-cent policy floor because FY2026E free cash flow to equity cannot fund a three-quarters distribution while the build stands [S0, S5, S8, S7, F43]. It is worth Rp1,791 before the liquidity discount. On the FY2022 reconciliation the red team asked for, we state the arithmetic rather than defend the base with a data point we cannot file: the same cost link, at the exposure share and pass-through the model uses, would have charged only about a sixth of the margin fall the FY2022 accounts show, so the link alone cannot reproduce that episode — the rest was volume loss and price timing [S8, F60]. At Brent near the deck's FY2026E level the base therefore assumes explicitly that the FY2022 outcome does not recur, and the evidence for it is the filed first-half margin, which printed above the audited FY2025 rate; the FY2022 outcome is carried in this bear and in the sensitivity grid, so a reader who does not accept that judgement has the number in front of them [S6, S5, S8]. Our bull case is the mirror: it assumes the adhesive and gravure mix holds and lifts margin four points, exactly the bear's four points the other way, the company uses its unused nameplate without expansion capex and takes share from imported ink as the rupiah weakens, and working capital releases three points, mirroring the bear's build; it is worth Rp4,134 before the discount [S0, S7, S3]. The base case is Rp2,509 and carries half the probability weight, with the two tails at a quarter each [S0]. The only asymmetries left are two, and both point against us rather than for us: the bear's payout cut has no bull counterpart, because a cut to the floor is a step change the board can take and a payout above the maximum already paid is not a policy any controller has signalled [S4, S7], and the convexity of a value that is linear in neither growth nor margin puts the weighted value of Rp2,736 nearly a tenth above the base scenario of Rp2,509, with the published target of Rp2,188 above the base scenario's own discounted value by the same proportion — which we disclose rather than smooth, and which is why the base-scenario value is shown next to the weighted one [S0].

The bear deserves emphasis because it sets how the rating should be read. The scenario values are struck before the liquidity discount, so the bear of Rp1,791 is above today's share price before the discount and below it once the same discount is applied: the market price sits between the discounted bear and the discounted base [S0, S6]. In other words, the downside case is the market price and the target is the distance between the two, which is the pass-through holding at roughly the audited FY2025 margin rather than at the filed margin [S0]. That is a thinner margin of safety than the headline upside suggests, and it is why the case rests on the dividend and the net-cash pile rather than on the target alone [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A full-year gross margin below the audited FY2025 rate would say the pass-through has stopped working, which is the bear case arriving early [S5, S6]. Inventory or receivables rising faster than sales through the December balance sheet would say the cash conversion is deteriorating rather than seasonal [S0, S6]. A dividend below the stated minimum, or a payout cut to fund working capital, would remove the reason to own the shares [S4, S7]. And a fourth quarter that misses the third quarter's run-rate while the margin holds would say the price carry is fading faster than the deck's Brent path implies, which is the core of the FY2027E flat-revenue call [S0].

The company is controlled through an offshore vehicle. Ink Color International Pte. Ltd. holds 51.0% and is disclosed as the majority and controlling shareholder, with Mr Winardi Pranatajaya as the ultimate beneficial owner [S7, F34]. The board is led at commissioner level by Harris Pranatajaya, with Tjia Hwie Tjin as a commissioner and Didik Susilo as the independent commissioner, and Anthoni Gunawan sits on the board of directors [S7, S3]. Insider holdings of 71.7% and a free float of 17.6% are consistent with a founding-family company that has never diluted control [S0].

The governance risk is the ordinary one for a controlled company, and the disclosures are better than the float implies. Related-party sales were IDR8.3bn in FY2025, a fraction of the IDR979.3bn of revenue, and related-party trade receivables at June were small relative to the third-party balance [S5, S6, F21]. There is an audit committee, an internal audit unit, a corporate secretary and a whistleblowing system, and the annual report states that no complaint of a Code of Ethics violation or indication of fraud was received through that system during the year [S7]. We found no litigation or administrative sanction disclosed in the filings reviewed, which is a statement about disclosure rather than proof that none exists [S5, S7].

The audit is clean and the dividend record is the main minority protection. The FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified opinion from the Ernst and Young member firm in Jakarta, signed in March 2026, with no qualification on going concern or on fixed-asset carrying values [S5]. The company has paid a cash dividend in every year of the record we hold, and the distribution out of FY2025 profit of Rp171 a share is the largest of them [S4, S5, F31]. The stated policy of a minimum of 20.0% of profit is a floor, and the actual payment of 75.0% shows the controlling shareholder takes cash out through the dividend rather than through related-party channels [S7, F43, F32].

On ESG, the exposure is the chemistry the company handles and the packaging it enables. The annual report describes water and energy efficiency, waste management on the reduce-reuse-recycle principle, and the treatment of hazardous waste from contaminated packaging and ink sludge, which are the relevant environmental items for a formulator that handles solvents [S7]. Eco-friendly product volumes reached 819 tonnes in FY2025 within total output of 14,727 tonnes, so the sustainable product line is real but small relative to the base [S7, F49, F15]. The social and governance disclosures are conventional for an Indonesian listed manufacturer: a small permanent workforce, a code of ethics, and a board with one independent commissioner [S7, F22].

The environmental profile of an ink formulator is dominated by solvents and by the fate of the printed package. Solvent-based inks release volatile organic compounds during printing and drying, so converters increasingly specify water-based or energy-curable systems, and a formulator that can supply them keeps the account. The packaging itself is the larger question for the customer: a multilayer flexible structure is hard to recycle, which is why brand owners are pushing mono-material designs and why the ink has to work on a different substrate. That shift is a product-mix opportunity for a formulator with technical service and a volume risk for one that sells only standard solvent inks.

The calendar is results and the dividend. The full-year audited accounts for FY2026, due by the end of the first quarter of 2027, will be the clean read on two things this note leaves open: whether the second half held the run-rate the first half set, and whether the September working-capital balance unwound at the year-end as it did last year [S0, S6, S7, S5]. The annual meeting in the middle of 2027 will set the dividend out of FY2026 profit, and the stated policy floor is the number to watch against the actual payout [S4, S7]. The Brent average for the fourth quarter is the highest-frequency marker of the input cost that sets the following year's margin, and the first-quarter interim report is the first read on collections after the year-end [S3, S6].

Between updates we monitor four numbers. The gross margin against the filed first-half rate tells us whether the pass-through is still working or whether the lag has become a squeeze [S6, S5]. Inventory and receivable days tell us whether the cash conversion is seasonal or deteriorating; the September print kept the flag at optics rather than manipulation, but a further rise from here would move it [S0, F62, F64, F65, F67]. The short-term bank loan balance tells us whether the working-capital build is being funded by debt that has to be renewed, and the net-cash pile against the FY2026 payout tells us how much of the dividend this year is coming out of the balance sheet rather than out of cash flow [S0, S6, F41]. And the declared dividend against both the policy floor and FCFE tells us whether the controlling shareholder still wants the cash out through the minority, and whether the payout is still covered [S0, F43].

bear.narrative: A raw-material spike is not passed through, as in FY2022 (F60): gross margin falls 4.0pp, a partial repeat of the 4.6pp fall the accounts show. Revenue growth slows by 5pp on a 10% customer loss (Supernova is 10% of sales [S6]) and Chinese import competition; working capital rises 3pp of sales as collections slow. The payout is cut to the 20% policy floor [S7, F43] because FY2026E free cash flow to equity cannot carry a 75% distribution while the working-capital build stands, and the multiple de-rates with the small-cap tape. bull.narrative: Adhesive and gravure mix shift lifts gross margin 4.0pp, the exact mirror of the bear's margin shock, on the already-improved base; the unused nameplate is used without expansion capex, and revenue growth runs 5pp above base as the company takes share from imported ink while the rupiah weakens [S7].
